extracted.intended_audience: journalism students and trainee reporters (news reporters learning beat reporting)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for reporting and writing short news pieces on weather and labor/strike beats, showing what facts, sources, tone, and structure to include. Uses newspaper examples to illustrate effective treatment, from front‑page forecasts to vivid scene reporting of strikes and storms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weather stories — universal interest
rubrics_metrics.description: The universal interest in the weather, which makes it the most common topic of conversation, is due to its effect upon health, business, and pleasure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat weather as high‑audience copy: consider impacts on varied readers (businessman, farmer, shopper, pleasure‑seeker). Frame stories around these effects to explain why readers should care.

rubrics_metrics.name: Place official forecasts prominently
rubrics_metrics.description: Official forecasts of the weather are given a place of prominence on the front page of most papers, and are read with interest by most readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include the official Weather Bureau forecast early and clearly (often front‑page). Attribute forecasts to the official source and present the forecast succinctly (e.g., 'Fair, continued cold tonight and Wednesday; freezing tonight').

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptable topics for weather pieces
rubrics_metrics.description: Besides the official reports, there is opportunity for weather stories of various kinds. The change of the seasons, extremes of heat and cold, storms, and unusual weather of any sort serve as subjects for weather stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report not only routine forecasts but also seasonal changes, extremes, storms, and rare phenomena (eclipses noted as astronomical but often covered by papers). Choose items that have local or human impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone and treatment — informative or lighter/colored
rubrics_metrics.description: Although the purely informative type of story is the usual one for weather, the subject may be treated in a lighter vein. There is often a chance for life and color whether the treatment be informative or more or less humorous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide desired tone: straight information vs. human/feature angle. Use anecdotes, small scenes, or humorous observations to enliven routine forecasts, but keep factual accuracy when informative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include specific measurements, times and forecaster commentary
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide temperature readings, times, and forecaster predictions (examples: exact temperature readings, times of contacts for an eclipse, forecaster's expectations for minimum temperature).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use precise numeric data and timestamps to support weather claims (e.g., 'temperature reading of 34° on Sept. 29', 'first contact at 9:35:28'). Attribute numbers to instruments/officials and explain likely trends (forecaster's reasoning).

rubrics_metrics.name: Local impacts and human‑interest detail
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe effects on transportation, business, social life and include human scenes and anecdotes (e.g., street car/service interruptions, ruined business, people slipping, couples in parks).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report concrete local consequences — traffic delays, business losses, school/transport disruption — plus human vignettes to show how readers are affected. Use specific incidents to illustrate broader impacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical context and comparisons
rubrics_metrics.description: Place present weather in historical perspective by listing past records and notable earlier storms to contextualize present events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give historical precedents and record comparisons (dates, amounts) to show significance. Use tables or lists of previous storms/temperatures when helpful for context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vivid descriptive reporting for storms and disasters
rubrics_metrics.description: Use descriptive, vivid language to convey the scene and danger (examples show dramatic phrasing describing falling walls, roaring crashes, burning tents, suffocation in tent colonies).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ strong sensory detail and concrete verbs to convey urgency and scale, but avoid sensationalizing facts. Balance vividness with verified detail about injuries and damage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use named authorities and experts
rubrics_metrics.description: Include observations and technical details from named experts (astronomers, forecasters, inspectors) and identify instruments or methods when relevant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attribute technical facts to identified experts (name and title) and, where useful, describe instruments or measurement methods (e.g., 'photo‑heliograph', 'observed by Prof. W.S. Eichelberger'). This increases credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report both sides in labor disputes
rubrics_metrics.description: Give statements and positions from both the workers/union and the merchants/company officials, including offers, refusals, and explanations of bargaining positions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance reporting by quoting and summarizing union leaders and employers, present offers on the table (e.g., arbitration, half‑holiday proposals) and reasons each side gives for its stance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detail specific demands and employer proposals
rubrics_metrics.description: Spell out concrete demands (e.g., a fifty‑four‑hour week, Saturday half‑holiday, time‑and‑a‑half for overtime) and exactly what merchants offered in response.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: List the precise terms being negotiated so readers understand the stakes. Present numerical proposals and counterproposals clearly and in comparable terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: List affected employers, locations and scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Name the larger houses and firms affected by the strike (several companies are listed) and specify where the tie‑up is practically complete.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide a roster of affected businesses and precise locations to convey the strike's extent. This helps readers and local businesses assess the disruption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Describe escalation, sympathetic actions and wider consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Note likely ripple effects (sympathetic strikes, Freight Handlers' Council involvement) and possible escalation (militia mobilization, machine‑gun sortie preparations in the Ludlow example).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report on related labor and civic bodies' responses and the potential for spread or reprisal. Explain short‑term and systemic consequences for industry and public order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Give chronological narrative and key incidents
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide a timeline of events, sequence of negotiations breaking off, immediate calling out of men, mass meetings, arrests and injuries, and decisions to continue or call off strikes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure labor stories with clear chronology: what happened first, next, and outcomes. Include notable incidents (riots, arrests, violence) to anchor the narrative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use first‑person quotations and economic detail to illustrate grievances
rubrics_metrics.description: Use direct quotes from workers (drivers' first‑person account of pay breakdown) and include economic calculations (percentage of fares, expenses, net take‑home) to show cause of grievances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include representative quotations that reveal motives and conditions. When economics are central, show calculations and figures that explain whether demands appear reasonable; attribute claims appropriately.
